Recover the planetary system that produced this signal: the number of
planets and each one's orbital parameters. The data is available to your
tools; you do not need it inlined here.

A submission passes only if it satisfies all four criteria at once: the
model must beat a flat line (delta-BIC), the residual scatter must be
within 1.5x the median reported uncertainty, the orbits must match the
underlying system, and the planet count must be right. A good statistical
fit at the wrong period fails.

Initial hypothesis: start with 1 planet at 73.07 d.

Why:
- The 73.07 d peak is overwhelmingly dominant (power 0.723, FAP ~ 0).
- It is well within the 211.9 d baseline, so it is constrained.
- The nearby 37.84 d peak is very plausibly the first harmonic / half-period relative of the 73 d signal, since 2 × 37.84 = 75.68 d, close to the main peak. Given the much stronger 73 d power, I would treat 37.84 d as an alias/harmonic candidate rather than the primary planet period.
- The short-period peaks near 0.63–1.08 d overlap the 1-day cadence/window structure and are not convincing planet candidates at this stage.
- No other longer-period peak is comparably significant.

So the simplest supported model is:
- Planet b: P ≈ 73.07 days

Please fit a 1-planet model at ~73.07 d first, then inspect residuals to see whether the 37.8 d feature survives as an independent planet or disappears as a harmonic/alias of the 73 d signal.
